extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology / literary studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and constructing the fabula: how to select and order events and actors, how duration and chronology operate (crisis vs development, ellipsis, parallelism), and how location/spatial oppositions contribute meaning. Emphasises structuralist classification and relation of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration: development form
rubrics_metrics.description: A development presents, in historical order, as much material as seems fit; the most important topic is the passing of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Development tends to require longer time spans and thus longer texts (novels). Global significance is built up slowly from strings of events; actors' insights and relationships take shape through the quality of events. Selection is still required (parts skipped, abbreviated, summarized) and different works vary greatly in how they represent development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration: crisis form
rubrics_metrics.description: The crisis form restricts the fabula to a brief period of the actor's life centered on a decisive moment; the crisis is representative of the actors and their relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis narratives (e.g., many modern/contemporary stories) focus on a central, informing event; because of their brevity they often need techniques to extend compass (recollections, references to past/future, sub-fabulas). In visual art ‘pregnant moment’ equivalents exist. The crisis form imposes selection and has implications for fabula construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of events (summary, omission, abbreviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fabula is always selected material: not an entire life but parts; selection techniques include skipping, abbreviation, and summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection choices carry meaning (e.g., Flaubert's laconic line about Emma's pregnancy signals its insignificance to her). Omitted events (ellipsis) can gain rhetorical or thematic force; deliberate omissions may leave gaps that shape reader interpretation (Robbe-Grillet example). Consider which events are presented and which are elided as an explicit criterion of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis / elimination as chronological technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination (ellipsis) causes gaps in chronology by omitting elements that belong in a series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipsis can be used to indicate insignificance (Flaubert), to create mystery or unreliable chronology (Robbe-Grillet's Voyeur omits a crucial event), or to focus representation. Ask what omitted events imply and how omissions are later filled or left ambiguous; ellipsis is a productive narrative device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology variation techniques (condensation, parallel development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time sequence may be varied by condensation of duration, elimination, or parallel development of several strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These techniques affect perceived chronology: condensation can compress long durations, parallel strands can criss-cross and make precise chronology impossible, and elimination creates gaps. Analyze how these techniques alter the fabula’s perceived continuity and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism and achronicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple, parallel strings of events can make it difficult or impossible to establish a single precise chronology (achronicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel or multiplying story lines (e.g., One Hundred Years of Solitude) can overwhelm readers’ attempts to keep track and can be used deliberately to produce effects (eternalizing time, blurring sequence). Consider whether chronology vagueness is significant for theme or characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical sequence vs chronological sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence is a logical concept distinct from chronological order; chronological and causal connections are not always interrelated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume temporal precedence implies qualitative or causal priority. Structural analysis benefits from distinguishing logical sequences (what must precede what conceptually) from chronological order (what happened when). Use this to expose ideological misconceptions (examples drawn from biblical creation readings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering effects on meaning (time span vs order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordering of events (chronological vs arranged) can change an event's significance and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the effect of presenting events in chronological order versus an alternative order: a brief meeting after a long estrangement has different implications than if it had occurred earlier. Examining ordering reveals differences between fabula and narrated story and affects readers' interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location inference and the reader’s supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Events happen somewhere; when a location is not explicitly stated readers will supply one (spatial imagination predominates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple cues (e.g., shopping cart + checkout) are sufficient for readers to infer place. Mapping where fabulas occur can reveal relations between event types, actor identities, and place. Note how minimal locational cues function and when the text relies on reader-supplied space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial oppositions and their semantic roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatial oppositions (inside/outside, city/country, high/low, far/near, open/closed, familiar/strange, safe/unsafe, accessible/inaccessible) often structure fabulas and carry associated connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions can suggest protection vs danger (inside/outside), iniquity vs innocence (city/country), or social hierarchy (kitchen/drawing-room). These contrasts are not fixed; meanings can reverse (city depicted as maddening vs idyllic). Use such oppositions to analyze thematic and ideological effects (Emma Bovary, Cheri, Upstairs Downstairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundaries and liminal/mediating locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Boundaries and transitional places (front door, shop as between inside/outside, sea as between society/solitude, beach, gardens, vehicles, roads) mediate oppositions and can function as critical structural sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundaries may connote access or barriers and can trap or facilitate actors. Liminal spaces often launch fabulas or suspend social order (transportation scenes in mysteries, sex in Flaubert). Analyze how such places operate structurally and symbolically (e.g., Texaco’s road as penetrative/destructive site).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vehicles and places of transition as narrative devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Trains, boats, carriages, planes and other vehicles frequently serve as settings that suspend social predictability and enable pivotal events (murder, sex, meetings, quarrels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transient locations temporarily break ordinary order and are narratively productive. Note their structuring potential: they are often used as neutral meeting grounds, sites of danger, or catalysts for plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositions are constructed; beware naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Spatial and other binary oppositions are constructions and may be ideologically loaded and flawed; they should not be naturalized in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deconstructive and ideological criticism shows oppositions’ instability. Use awareness of constructed oppositions as a critical tool: confront expected oppositions with your own and use differences to critique ideological readings rather than simply confirming binaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors: classification and actantial modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors are primarily handled by classification (actantial roles) rather than the same selection criteria used for events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter endorses Greimas’s sixfold actantial model (subject, object, sender, receiver, helper, opponent) and resists later substitutions that collapse distinctions (anti-actant/co-actant). Keep possibilities such as duplication of principal actant and distinctions between autonomous anti-subjects and incidental opponents in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuralist approach as methodological rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe elements (events, actors, time, location) in relation to one another rather than as isolated units; classification is instrumental to insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make ordering principles explicit when treating determined relationships between classes of phenomena. Classification should be used only insofar as it enhances understanding of texts; treat typologies as starting points for critique, not endpoints.
